solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: James embracing that French character in AYLI

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so one piece wraps its arms around the other

parts.note: JAS is the old written abbreviation of James
que is French for 'that'

explanation.surface: Someone called James hugging a French figure from a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: AYLI is short for As You Like It, Shakespeare's comedy; JAS is a traditional abbreviation of James, as on old letters and gravestones.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaques is the melancholy lord in Shakespeare's comedy who gives the famous 'All the world's a stage' speech.

clue.text: Harriers bound to fountains

parts.note: to bound is to leap
jets of water, as from a fountain

explanation.surface: Hunting dogs or hawks heading off towards some fountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harriers' suggests hounds, birds of prey or runners; here it is the British Harrier aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawker Siddeley Harrier was a famous vertical take-off military plane, popularly called a jump jet.

clue.text: Mildly amused Jack left jacuzzi with half the liquor spilt

indicators.note: spilt things are scattered about, so the combined letters land in a new order
something that has left has departed, so that letter is gone from the word

parts.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack; this letter is removed
the hot tub, which loses its J

indicators.note: half asks for only the first part of the word, the rest discarded

parts.note: the first half: three of the word's six letters

explanation.surface: A man called Jack, faintly amused, climbs out of a hot tub after spilling half his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like the man's name, but it is the J to be removed from JACUZZI; ACUZZI plus LIQ are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A quizzical look shows mild puzzlement or wry amusement, the expression of someone faintly entertained.

clue.text: Declines, as Stanley and Beatrice lose their head

indicators.note: losing a head means the top, the opening letter, is cut off

parts.note: a couple surnamed Webb; Beatrice Webb was the Fabian social reformer

explanation.surface: A couple named Stanley and Beatrice are going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken together the pair are the Webbs; Beatrice Webb and her husband (Sidney, in fact) founded the London School of Economics.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide ebbs as it goes out, so to ebb is to decline, dwindle or fade away.

clue.text: Small wife trembled outside and complained loudly

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: to quake is to tremble
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A little wife shook outdoors and grumbled noisily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' reads as outdoors in the surface; in the wordplay QUAKED goes outside the W.
explanation.definitionFit: To squawk is to give a harsh cry like a parrot; informally it means to protest noisily.

clue.text: Tenderest feelings shot as temporary solution

parts.note: the quick is the most sensitive flesh, as in 'cut to the quick'
a fix is a shot of a drug

explanation.surface: Someone's deepest emotions are wrecked, offered as a stopgap remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like 'ruined'; it is a dose or injection, a fix. 'Cut to the quick' means hurt in one's deepest feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick fix is an expedient patch-up that deals with a problem only for the moment.

clue.text: Wrecked taxi, he pays for throttle

indicators.note: a wrecked thing is smashed apart, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A man who crashed a cab must pay for the accelerator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throttle' sounds like the car part to be paid for after the crash; it is the verb meaning to strangle.
explanation.definitionFit: To throttle someone is to choke them, cutting off breath, which is to suffocate or starve of oxygen.

clue.text: Hillock appearing when returning from stroll on Kerrera

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so read right to left
coming from within a phrase means the letters are drawn out of its run of text

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the three words

explanation.surface: A small hill comes into view on the way back from a walk on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Kerrera is a small island off Oban in western Scotland; written backwards the answer straddles its end and the end of 'stroll'.
explanation.definitionFit: A knoll is a small rounded hill or mound, the same thing as a hillock.

clue.text: Fools society girls around half the week

indicators.note: to go around something is to encircle it, one piece enclosing another

parts.note: debs are debutantes, young women entering high society

indicators.note: half asks for only the first part of the word, the rest dropped

parts.note: the first half: two of the word's four letters

explanation.surface: Debutantes spend half the week playing tricks on people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fools' looks like a verb, as in deceives; it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A dweeb is slang for a feeble, socially awkward or stupid person, a nerd or idiot.

clue.text: An accepted truth that amateur team receives award

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for amateur
a cricket or football team is an eleven, XI in Roman numerals
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: It is a known fact that the amateur side is getting a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: A side of eleven players is written XI, and the Order of Merit is a high British honour given by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a statement taken as self-evidently true, a basic premise that needs no proof.

clue.text: 9lb wrecked for private letter container

indicators.note: a wrecked thing is smashed apart, so the letters are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: a cross-reference to the answer of 9 down
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nine pounds of something gets smashed up for a personal postbox.
explanation.walkthrough: '9lb' reads as a weight, but 9 stands for the answer at 9 down, joined with the letters LB.
explanation.definitionFit: A mailbox is a box for receiving letters, and a private one belongs to a single household.

clue.text: Make things better for one member having turned over

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: turned means changed or altered, so the letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician who changed sides makes things better for somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned over' reads as a phrase for switching sides; 'turned' alone acts on OVER.
explanation.definitionFit: To improve is to enhance or raise the quality of something, making it superior.

clue.text: Apple providing music

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a modern variety of eating apple
second meaning: the improvised musical style

explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple providing music' suggests an Apple device or app; instead it is a variety of the fruit sold in British supermarkets.
explanation.definitionFit: Jazz is a branded cross-bred apple variety, and also the syncopated, improvised genre born in New Orleans.

clue.text: Scotsman confused by clue for commercial horse-racing group

parts.note: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman

indicators.note: confused things are muddled, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scot, baffled by a crossword hint about a racing organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' looks like it describes the Scotsman, but it rearranges the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jockey Club is the long-established British racing body that now owns and runs major racecourses as a business.

clue.text: Official bulletin about love with gents in France. That's a one-off

parts.note: C is circa, Latin for about
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
MM abbreviates messieurs, French for gentlemen
a one-off is the only one of its kind

explanation.surface: A formal announcement about romance among Frenchmen, said to be a one-time event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the word linking bulletin to its subject, but it supplies the C; MM is the French counterpart of Messrs.
explanation.definitionFit: A communique is an official statement or report issued to the press or public.

clue.text: Magnate from outskirts of Torbay gets company working

indicators.note: outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the two end letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters
Co is the abbreviation for company
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A business baron from the edge of a Devon resort gets his firm running.
explanation.walkthrough: Torbay is the seaside area of Devon in south-west England that includes Torquay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tycoon is a wealthy, powerful businessperson, the same as a magnate or industrial baron.

clue.text: Provided backward judge is covering an island race

indicators.note: going backward means running in the opposite direction, right to left

parts.note: 'provided' means on condition that, if
J is the abbreviation for judge

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie over and around it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: If a slow-witted judge is reporting on a race held on some island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a contest, but it means a people; 'backward' looks like an insult to the judge but turns IF round.
explanation.definitionFit: Fijians are the people of Fiji, a nation of islands in the South Pacific, so an island people.

clue.text: First lieutenant drops sultan for Pharaoh queen

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it fall away, so those letters are removed

parts.note: the fifteen letters taken as written
the six letters removed, from wherever they fall

explanation.surface: A senior naval officer abandons an Ottoman ruler in favour of an Egyptian queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The six letters of SULTAN are struck out of FIRST LIEUTENANT wherever they occur, and the nine left over are rearranged; no separate anagram signal is given.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefertiti was the chief wife of the Egyptian ruler Akhenaten, famous for her painted bust in Berlin.

clue.text: Delay execution of agent, always up about one

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative or agent

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: ever means always
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Postpone hanging a spy who is forever up to something.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the agent the condemned man; REP is a sales agent and 'up' turns EVER over in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To reprieve a prisoner is to postpone or cancel the carrying out of a sentence, especially a death sentence.

clue.text: Imposing portals off-stage — way in

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Grand doorways backstage provide the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-stage' reads as backstage, but 'off' rearranges STAGE; 'way in' also sounds like a definition of a gateway but is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Gateways are large entrances, often grand arched or gated openings, so impressive doors or portals.

clue.text: One fruit and some others for workman

parts.note: a plum is a single fruit
part of BERRIES, the other fruits, cut short

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit and a few more, handed to a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' does double duty: one fruit is PLUM, and some of the other fruits are part of BERRIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumber is a tradesman who fits and repairs water pipes, a skilled manual worker.

clue.text: All the employees by a Hebridean isle

parts.note: the staff are the whole workforce
taken as written

explanation.surface: The whole workforce standing beside a small Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hebrides are the islands off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is a small uninhabited island in the Inner Hebrides, home of the basalt Fingal's Cave.

clue.text: Strict consumers putting half the eggs in vehicles

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, enclosed

parts.note: vans are vehicles

indicators.note: half asks for only the first part of the word, the rest dropped

parts.note: the first half: two of the word's four letters

explanation.surface: Fussy customers loading half the eggs into vans.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the eggs are exactly what such strict eaters refuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Vegans follow a rigorous diet, eating no meat, fish, eggs, dairy or other animal products.

clue.text: Over-sentimental Cockney song and dance. Not half!

indicators.note: not half means one half is left out, so only the other half remains

parts.note: the British party song with actions; London-flavoured, hence Cockney

explanation.surface: A soppy London singalong and dance; 'Not half!' is the Cockney cry of emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The British hokey cokey is the hokey pokey elsewhere; 'Not half!' is Cockney slang for 'definitely', but here it removes the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Hokey is an informal word for mawkish, sentimental or contrived, especially in a corny way.

clue.text: Novel making editor turn cross

parts.note: ED is the abbreviation for editor
to wind is to turn, as with a handle
a rood is a cross or crucifix, especially in a church

explanation.surface: A new book makes its editor angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new, and 'cross' like angry; they are a book and a crucifix.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mystery of Edwin Drood is Charles Dickens's final novel, left unfinished at his death in 1870.

clue.text: Restaurant employee drops one drink

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so that letter falls out

parts.note: a waiter serves tables in a restaurant
I is the Roman numeral one; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A waiter lets a glass fall to the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops one drink' paints a clumsy waiter; the I for one is what goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Water is the most basic beverage, the clear liquid people drink to quench thirst.

clue.text: Party leader's inner strong desire

indicators.note: the inner part is what lies within, so the opening letter is shed

parts.note: a purge is the party leader's clear-out of disloyal members

explanation.surface: A political leader's deep-seated craving.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is uncertain: one reading takes a party leader's purge of rivals and drops its first letter to leave the inside part.
explanation.definitionFit: An urge is a strong impulse or longing to do something, a powerful craving.

clue.text: Half a lozenge upset French novelist

indicators.note: in a down clue, set upside down means read from bottom to top
half of a phrase is just a portion of its letters, taken from within

parts.note: the opening four of the phrase's eight letters

explanation.surface: Half a throat sweet made a French writer ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like 'made unwell'; in this down entry it turns the letters upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Emile Zola was the French naturalist novelist of Germinal and author of the 'J'accuse' letter.

clue.text: Auction item — one that's quite odd

parts.note: an means one, the indefinite article

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so the letters fall into an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lot under the hammer that is rather peculiar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite odd' reads as 'rather strange'; 'odd' acts on QUITE instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiques, old collectable objects of value, are typically sold to bidders at auction houses.

clue.text: "Kiss and Love" in a quote about strange things

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
about means turned around, facing the other way

parts.note: taken as written
to cite is to quote
X is a kiss, as at the end of a letter
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A song titled Kiss and Love appears in a citation about curiosities.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the two words look like a song title, but each is a separate piece; 'in' and 'about' both look like plain prepositions.
explanation.definitionFit: Exotica are unusual, foreign or curious objects collected for their strangeness.

clue.text: Screamed "Quiet!" and "It smelt bad", we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so go by the sound

parts.note: SH is a call for quiet and reeked means smelt bad

explanation.surface: Someone yelled for silence and complained of a stink.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, the hush and the past tense of 'reek' run into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To shriek is to give a shrill piercing cry, which is to scream.

clue.text: Differs showing V-sign

parts.note: taken as written
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Someone disagrees by making a rude two-fingered gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: The V-sign is a rude British gesture; here V and 'sign' are separate pieces, the sign being astrological.
explanation.definitionFit: To vary is to be different or change, so 'varies' matches 'differs' as a verb.
